title: Consumer Responses to Advertising: The Effects of Ad Content, Emotions, and Attitude toward the Ad on Viewing Time
finding: Across a sample of prime-time commercials (analysis across ads, simulated zapping/zipping as viewing time), the authors show a chain of effects: ad content -> emotional reactions -> attitude toward the ad -> actual viewing time. No effect sizes in the abstract.
why_for_us: Staying is driven by the feeling the first shots create, not by the claim: the first seconds of an episode should produce an emotion (amusement, recognition of a notary's daily pain), and only then information.

title: Discrimination Vs. Avoidance: “Zipping” of Television Commercials
finding: Lab and field studies of fast-forwarding: per authors most viewers zip indiscriminately to avoid all commercials and few evaluate an ad before zipping; block zipping dominates; zipping is lowest for the first commercial in the first pod and highest in the last pod. No percentages in the abstract.
why_for_us: Once content is recognised as 'an ad', it is skipped as a category without being judged: the first frame of an episode must not look like advertising (no packshot, no logo card, no stock-ad look).

title: To Zap or Not to Zap: A Study of the Determinants of Channel Switching During Commercials
finding: Telemeter data from a single-source household panel (two product categories; logit + hazard model): per authors about 35% of households form a zap-prone segment; zapping is J-shaped in prior exposures with a minimum around 14 exposures; a brand-differentiating message slightly but significantly lowers zapping; 15 s and 30 s ads do not differ in expected share of time watched, but 15 s ads reach the overexposure threshold sooner.
why_for_us: Category users zap less, so the opening should signal 'this is about notarial work' at once to keep the right 65%; rotate openings before the same cut is seen too often, especially the short 6-15 s versions.

title: Why Do Consumers Stop Viewing Television Commercials? Two Experiments on the Influence of Moment-to-Moment Entertainment and Information Value
finding: Two experiments with moment-to-moment measures: entertainment value at a given moment lowers and information value raises the probability of stopping viewing at that moment; per authors the two have a strong multiplicative effect on the stop probability. No numbers in the abstract.
why_for_us: Do not open with a dense informational statement (law, feature list); put entertainment first and deliver information in moments that are also entertaining, because information without entertainment is where viewers leave.

title: Advertising Content and Television Advertising Avoidance
finding: Set-top-box data, proportional hazards model of the 'Passive/Active Zap': per authors 27% of eligible commercial breaks are interrupted by such a zap; avoidance is lower for movie ads and higher for ads for websites, auto insurance and women's clothing, and it rises with repeated exposure to the same creative and later in the evening.
why_for_us: Ads that look like entertainment (movie trailers) are avoided least and ads for websites/services most: a micro-drama should open like a trailer for a story, not like a pitch for a web service; vary the creative because repeats raise avoidance.

title: The Effect of Content on Zapping in TV Advertising
finding: Zapping data of over 2,500 German TV viewers matched to 1,315 spots (308 brands, 96 categories): per authors ad creativity is associated with less zapping, while a strong information focus and a prominent or early integration of branding elements are associated with more zapping; effects differ for utilitarian vs hedonic and search vs experience goods; a second study identifies irritation (relative to enjoyment) as the central mechanism.
why_for_us: Strongest recent field evidence for our decision: no prominent logo and no information-heavy lead in the first seconds; test separately because our product is utilitarian, where the authors report the effects differ.

title: An Integrative Approach to Determinants of Pre-Roll Ad Acceptance and Their Relative Impact: Evidence from Big Data
finding: Clickstream data of 2,078,090 users of a South Korean online video platform: per authors acceptance (not skipping) of skippable pre-roll ads depends on personal, situational and contextual factors that change how much the ad impedes the viewer's goal. The abstract gives no coefficients.
why_for_us: Skipping is partly decided by the viewer's situation, not the creative: judge a hook against its own placement (feed, pre-roll, email), not against one global benchmark.

title: Temporal Certainty and Skippable In-Stream Commercials: Effects of Ad Length, Timer, and Skip-ad Button on Irritation and Skipping Behavior
finding: Two experiments: showing a timer (known ad length) reduces irritation for short commercials, but when a skip button is present temporal certainty increases irritation for both short and long ads; higher irritation leads to a higher skipping rate and lower ad effectiveness, per authors.
why_for_us: Irritation is the route to skipping; for non-skippable 6-15 s cuts state or show the short length, and in skippable placements do not count on the countdown to hold people - the content of the first 5 s must.

title: Empowering Online Advertisements by Empowering Viewers with the Right to Choose: The Relative Effectiveness of Skippable Video Advertisements on YouTube
finding: Google's own randomized experiments on YouTube TrueView (skip after 5 s), with effectiveness measured by propensity to search for ad-related terms: per authors skippable ads may be as effective per impression as non-skippable ones and viewers strongly prefer them. Industry-authored (Google).
why_for_us: A skippable placement does not have to cost effect per impression, so the first 5 s should carry the brand idea in some form (spoken or shown in the story) for those who leave at the skip point. Treat as vendor evidence.

title: Understanding the effectiveness of video ads: a measurement study
finding: Akamai traces (about 65 million viewers, 362 million videos, 257 million ads, 33 providers; quasi-experimental matching): per authors a mid-roll ad is 18.1% more likely to complete than a pre-roll; a 15 s ad is 2.9% more likely to complete than a 20 s ad, which is 3.9% more likely than a 30 s ad; about one-third of abandoners leave in the first quarter of the ad and about two-thirds by the half-way point.
why_for_us: Abandonment is front-loaded: for a 15 s cut the first 3-4 s decide a third of the losses; use 15 s rather than 30 s versions where completion matters.

title: Understanding Interactive Online Advertising: Congruence and Product Involvement in Highly and Lowly Arousing, Skippable Video Ads
finding: A pretest and three studies on skippable ads: per authors high-arousal ads are watched longer and are more effective when congruent with the surrounding content; the viewer's product involvement determines how intrusive high- and low-arousal ads feel. No effect sizes in the abstract.
why_for_us: Open with an arousing moment (conflict, deadline, mistake at the desk) and place the cuts next to congruent professional content; involved viewers (notaries) may tolerate a calmer opening than outsiders.

title: Increasing the Efficacy of Emotional Appeal Ads on Online Video-Watching Platforms: The Effects of Goals and Emotional Approach Tendency on Ad-Skipping Behavior
finding: Three experiments with real-time skip tracking: emotional-appeal ads are skipped less by viewers who came for emotional (vs informational) videos, mediated by empathy; among viewers who do not seek emotional experiences the effect reverses, per authors.
why_for_us: A sceptical professional in information-seeking mode may skip an emotional opening faster: for LinkedIn/email cuts prefer a concrete professional situation over a sentimental one; keep emotional openings for entertainment feeds.

title: Moment-to-Moment Optimal Branding in TV Commercials: Preventing Avoidance by Pulsing
finding: Zapping plus eye tracking on 31 commercials with nearly 2,000 participants (dynamic probit model): per authors dispersion of viewers' attention strongly predicts avoidance; central on-screen brand positions (but not brand size) further promote avoidance; brand pulsing - several short brand appearances at constant total exposure - decreases avoidance significantly, confirmed in simulations and a controlled experiment with re-edited commercials.
why_for_us: Show the brand in brief repeated pulses inside the story (screen of the app, a mug, a spoken name) rather than one long central logo card; keep every shot with a single clear focal point so attention does not disperse.

title: DO NOT WAIT TO REVEAL THE BRAND NAME: The Effect of Brand-Name Placement on Television Advertising Effectiveness
finding: Experiment with award-winning TV ads re-edited to reveal the brand name at the beginning or at the end: per authors advertising is more effective with the name at the beginning, because the name becomes associated with the evaluative content of the ad; the effect did not run through ad liking, memory for the brand name or accessibility of ad content.
why_for_us: If the brand appears only in the last frame, the good feeling built by the story is not attached to it: name or show the product early in a light way so that what follows is filed under the brand.

title: On the Development and Strength of Category-Brand Associations in Memory
finding: Experiment on 'mystery ads' (brand identified only at the end): per authors they build stronger category-to-brand associations in memory than identical ads identifying the brand early, and they work best for novel, unfamiliar brands.
why_for_us: Counter-evidence to early branding for an unknown brand like ours: a late reveal can tie 'software for notaries' to the brand name - but only for viewers who stay to the end, so use it in formats with high completion (email, organic followers), not in skippable ads.

title: The Efficacy of Brand-Execution Tactics in TV Advertising, Brand Placements, and Internet Advertising
finding: Multiple studies across TV ads, internet video ads and in-programme placements: per author showing the brand early and often and having at least one verbal mention enhances brand recall; evidence is mixed for verbal frequency and there is no support for the brand merely being on screen for a long time.
why_for_us: For recall plan: brand visible in the first seconds, repeated several times, and said aloud at least once (also in captions for sound-off viewing); long static logo time adds nothing.

title: Breaking Through Fast-Forwarding: Brand Information and Visual Attention
finding: Two eye-tracking studies and a choice study: fast-forwarding viewers attend heavily to screen centre; per authors ads with brand information at screen centre still create brand memory even with a 95% reduction in frames and no audio, whereas brand information elsewhere is of virtually no value; central branding can affect attitude and actual choice.
why_for_us: For people who scroll past or watch muted, only what sits in the centre of the frame registers: place the product name/screen in the centre of an early frame and keep corner logos as a supplement only. Note tension with Teixeira et al. (central brand raises zapping).

title: Brand recognition in television advertising: The influence of brand presence and brand introduction
finding: Analysis the authors call a meta-analysis of responses to 25 TV ads from 50,000 respondents: brand recognition rises linearly with brand presence and falls the later the brand is introduced; the authors conclude a brand should be present for about two-thirds of the ad.
why_for_us: Supports early introduction and long presence for recognition; the two-thirds figure rests on 25 ads in a regional journal, so treat it as a rough upper guide, not a rule.

title: Humor in Television Advertising: A Moment‐to‐Moment Analysis
finding: Moment-to-moment analysis of humorous TV ads: per authors a dynamic transformation of surprise into humour lies at the heart of perceived humour, and key features of the moment-to-moment surprise and humour traces drive overall humour judgments. No numbers in the abstract.
why_for_us: A funny opening needs a surprise that resolves quickly: set up an expectation in the first shot (solemn notarial office) and break it within seconds; a joke without a preceding surprise will not register as humour.

title: The Effects of Incongruity, Surprise and Positive Moderators on Perceived Humor in Television Advertising
finding: Two studies testing an incongruity-resolution model on TV ads: surprise from incongruity is necessary but not sufficient for humour; playfulness, ease of resolving the incongruity and warmth decide whether surprise becomes humour, and with other context the same surprise can turn into fear, per authors; schema familiarity moderates the surprise.
why_for_us: An incongruous opening must be playful, warm and easy to 'get', otherwise the surprise reads as unease; the incongruity works only against a schema the audience knows well - a notary's office routine is such a schema for our viewers.

title: Managing the Power of Curiosity for Effective Web Advertising Strategies
finding: Simulated internet experiment with clickstream tracking: per authors a curiosity-generating ad raises interest and learning relative to an ad giving detailed product information; it improves the quality (time and attention) rather than the quantity of search; they recommend four elements: highlight a knowledge gap, give a hint, allow time and assure that the resolving information will come.
why_for_us: Open with a gap plus a hint ('what did the client forget to bring?') and visibly promise the answer within the episode; a gap with no hint or no promised resolution does not do the job.

title: Curiosity-inducing advertising: how positive emotions and expectations drive the effect of curiosity on consumer evaluations of products
finding: Two experiments comparing curiosity triggers (information gaps, ambiguity, novelty): per authors not all commonly used triggers actually stimulate curiosity; where curiosity arises, its positive effect on product attitude runs through heightened positive expectations and sometimes positive affect - an expectation-driven, rather uncritical evaluation.
why_for_us: Do not assume a vague or merely odd opening creates curiosity - test it; and because curiosity raises expectations, the payoff must meet them, or a sceptical audience will feel baited.

title: Effects of Interestingness on Evaluations of TV Commercials
venue: Journal of Current Issues & Research in Advertising
finding: Study of TV commercials relating executional features to interest while watching: interest arises from an information gap the viewer must fill (unexpected plot ending, brand identified late, message understandable only late); interesting commercials produce more favourable attitudes toward the ad and the brand, per author.
why_for_us: Structure each episode so that something is not yet understood until late; this is the attention-holding argument for delaying the full message (not necessarily the brand).

title: Before the skip option: impact of facial presence on video view completions
finding: Platform data on 3,498 skippable video ads across 685 channels and 23 product categories: per authors a lower share of facial presence before the skip option is associated with greater view counts; for utilitarian products less facial presence before the skip point goes with more views, while for hedonic products facial presence is not significantly related to qualified views. Correlational.
why_for_us: Directly on our question 'face in the first frame?': for a utilitarian product do not fill the first 5 s with a talking head; open on the situation/object (document, screen, desk) and bring the face in after. Very recent, uncited, observational.

title: How celebrity status and gaze direction in ads drive visual attention to shape consumer decisions
finding: Lab study with 77 participants (eye tracking, pupillometry, computational choice modelling): gaze cueing and celebrity endorsement both shift where viewers look and which option they choose; per authors the celebrity effect acts as a head start and a faster rate in evidence accumulation.
why_for_us: A character's gaze steers the viewer: in the opening frame have the character look at the thing we want noticed (the screen, the document) rather than away from it. Static ads, not video.

title: Absence Makes the Mind Grow Sharper: Effects of Element Omission on Subsequent Recall
finding: Series of experiments: an ad that deliberately omits a key element produces better recall than the same ad containing it, even with exposure times as short as four seconds; the gain is specific to what was omitted (omitting a brand-related element improves brand recall, a category-related one category recall), per authors.
why_for_us: For 6 s cuts and thumbnails: leave one expected element out so the viewer completes it (unfinished brand phrase, cropped familiar object); choose the omitted element by what we want remembered.

title: Can muted video advertising be as effective as video advertising with sound?
finding: OpenAlex holds no abstract for this article; the record's title and keywords (subtitles, brand recall, brand recognition, ad liking, audio branding, visual narrative) show it compares muted and with-sound video ads on recall, recognition and liking. No result can be stated from the record.
why_for_us: The one study in the set that tests our exact sound-off question; read the full text before fixing the caption policy for Facebook/LinkedIn autoplay.

title: Enhancing television advertising: same-language subtitles can improve brand recall, verbal memory, and behavioral intent
venue: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science
finding: OpenAlex holds no abstract; per the title, same-language subtitles on TV advertising can improve brand recall, verbal memory and behavioural intent (design and effect sizes not available from the record).
why_for_us: Burn in same-language (Polish) captions from the first second, including the spoken brand name: per title they help recall even with sound on. Verify numbers in the full text.

title: Strategies for Creating Successful Soundless Video Advertisements: Speaking Volumes Through Silence
finding: Qualitative study (prior research, ads from articles and an agency dataset, interviews with advertising professionals): the authors derive four strategies with operational tactics for ads viewed without sound. The abstract does not list the strategies and reports no effect data.
why_for_us: Checklist source for designing the episode to be understood muted (visual storytelling, on-screen text); practitioner-derived, not an effect test.

title: The Sound Factor in Autoplay Mobile Video Ads
venue: European Advertising Academy (Advances in Advertising Research Vol. XI)
finding: Book chapter without abstract in OpenAlex; keywords (mobile advertising, expectancy violation theory, mere exposure effect, advertising recall, brand attitude, consumer attitudes toward advertising) indicate an experiment on sound-on vs sound-off autoplay of mobile video ads. No result can be stated from the record.
why_for_us: Relevant to whether an episode should start with sound in autoplay feeds (unexpected sound as an expectancy violation); needs the full text before use.

title: Small sounds, big impact: sonic logos and their effect on consumer attitudes, emotions, brands and advertising placement
finding: Pretest plus two experiments with a happy and a sad sonic logo: the happy logo produced higher ad attitude; attitudes were mediated by felt emotion and moderated by placement - per authors a sad sonic logo did better at the beginning and a happy one at the end of the ad.
why_for_us: If 'Komputerku' gets a sound signature, a bright/happy one belongs at the end of the episode (and of the 6 s cut), not at the start; a sombre sting would go first.

title: Music to the ears: the role of sonic branding in advertising
finding: Experiments on sonic logos in ads: per authors they evoke positive emotions, stimulate engagement and enrich brand experience, especially among people high in emotion-based decision-making. No effect sizes in the abstract.
why_for_us: A short sound mark can add positive affect, but the benefit is concentrated among emotion-driven deciders - expect less from it with a sceptical, analytical professional audience.

title: The Effect of Background Music on Ad Processing: A Contingency Explanation
finding: Experiment: message reception depends on the interplay of the music's attention-gaining value and its congruency with the message; attention-getting music enhances reception only when it evokes message-congruent thoughts, per authors.
why_for_us: An attention-grabbing musical start helps only if it fits what the scene says (office, paperwork, tension); a catchy but unrelated track at the opening pulls processing away from the message.

title: Creating the Contrast: The Influence of Silence and Background Music on Recall and Attribute Importance
finding: Radio-ad experiment: cutting from music to silence just before and during a key piece of information increases its retention compared with music throughout or silence throughout, most when the item is the last in a series; ads with no music at all were not recalled better overall than ads with music throughout.
why_for_us: Drop the music under the one line that must be remembered (product name or the key benefit) - contrast, not silence as such, does the work; best on the last item, i.e. near the end card.

title: Music to Your Brain: Background Music Changes Are Processed First, Reducing Ad Message Recall
finding: Two experiments (ads for six brands; then two ads with reduced change frequency): message recall is higher with background music that changes less often harmonically and texturally; per authors recall for new, unfamiliar brands suffers more from music interference than for established brands.
why_for_us: As an unfamiliar brand we are in the vulnerable group: under dialogue in the first seconds use steady, low-change music or none, and avoid musical 'events' on top of the brand line.

title: The effectiveness of human vs. AI voice-over in short video advertisements: A cognitive load theory perspective
venue: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
finding: OpenAlex holds no abstract; title and keywords (short video advertising, cognitive load, subtitles, purchase intention) show a comparison of human and AI voice-over in short video ads framed by cognitive load, with subtitles as a factor. No result can be stated from the record.
why_for_us: Directly relevant because our series is AI-generated with synthetic voices: read the full text before deciding on AI narration plus captions in the opening seconds.

title: The Effects of Length, Content, and Repetition on Television Commercial Effectiveness
finding: Lab experiment with novel commercials, multiple exposures and several outcome measures: informational 15 s ads were as effective as informational 30 s ads in several situations and can stand alone, while emotional 30 s ads were superior to emotional 15 s ads for learning the brand name and for attitude, per authors.
why_for_us: Short 6-15 s cuts should carry an informational point (one concrete benefit for the office); the emotional story needs the longer 60-90 s episode and loses when squeezed.

title: The Effects of Commercial Length On Advertising Impact: What Short Advertisements Can and Cannot Deliver
finding: Experiment comparing 7-, 15-, 30- and 60-second versions of the same commercials (recall, liking, brand attitude, biometrics): per authors 7 s ads were almost as effective as 15 s ads on unaided recall and 60 percent as effective as 30 s ads - diminishing returns to length for recall and for liking.
why_for_us: A 6-7 s cut buys most of the recall of a 15 s cut, so make 6 s and 30 s versions rather than 6 s and 15 s; do not expect the 6 s cut to build liking.

title: Cost Per Second: The Relative Effectiveness of 15- and 30-Second Television Advertisements
finding: Ad-test data from Australia, the US and the UK: recall and likeability of 15 s ads are approximately 80 percent of those of 30 s ads, while correct brand identification is equal; per authors better branding execution in 15 s ads compensates for their length.
why_for_us: Short cuts keep up only when branding is tight: in the 6-15 s versions the brand must be unmistakable (seen and said), even if the long episode brands lightly.

title: Comparing the Effectiveness of Executlonal Elements in TV Advertising: 15- versus 30-second Commercials
finding: Copy-testing agency data on a large number of TV commercials, 24 executional elements, recall and persuasion as outcomes: per authors some elements that work in a 15 s format are less effective in 30 s and vice versa. The abstract does not name the elements.
why_for_us: A short cut is not a trimmed long ad: choose devices for the 6-15 s versions separately and test them separately from the full episode.

title: Six-Second Advertisements On Television: Best Practices For Capturing Visual Attention
finding: Industry study of more than 3,000 six-second TV ads against 15 s and 30 s ads on visual attention: per authors the sixes were run in better pod positions and dayparts, which contributed positively to their performance. No attention figures in the abstract.
why_for_us: Reported strong attention for 6 s ads is partly a placement effect, so compare our 6 s and 15 s cuts in the same placement before concluding that shorter holds attention better.

title: Strategies for More Effective Six-Second Video Advertisements: Making the Most Of 144 Frames
finding: Qualitative study (prior research, an agency dataset, press articles, social media, practitioner interviews): the authors set out several actionable strategies for crafting six-second ads. The abstract does not list them and reports no effect data.
why_for_us: Source of working rules for the 6 s bumper cut of each episode; practitioner-derived, so use as hypotheses to test.

title: Influence of Native Video Advertisement Duration and Key Elements on Advertising Effectiveness in Mobile Feeds
finding: Lab experiment with EEG and eye tracking, N=40 in four groups (6 s with titles/logos/texts, 15 s with, 15 s without, 30 s without): participants felt more positive watching 6 s in-feed ads than 15 s or 30 s ones but remembered them worse; attention went to the key elements (title, logo, text) rather than to the ad content.
why_for_us: In feed, on-screen title/logo/text draw the eye more than the picture: write the opening caption as the hook itself. Small sample (10 per cell) and a journal of modest standing.

title: Advertising creativity and repetition: Recall, wearout and wearin effects
finding: Experiment with creative vs control commercials embedded in a TV programme and a one-week follow-up: creative ads show higher recall (the advantage shrinks with repeated exposures), are liked more, wear in faster and are less susceptible to wearout, per authors.
why_for_us: A genuinely creative opening can be repeated across episodes as a series signature with less fatigue than a plain one; still plan variants, since the recall edge narrows with repetition.

title: YouTube marketing: how marketers' video optimization practices influence video views
finding: Scraped YouTube trending list, N=4,398 videos, text and sentiment analysis: per author more information in the title is negatively associated with views, intensity of negative emotional sentiment in the title positively; more information in the description positively; tags show an inverted U with a turning point at 17 tags. Correlational, trending videos only.
why_for_us: Keep episode titles short and emotionally charged rather than descriptive, and move the informative text to the description; do not read this as proof for a small professional audience.

title: Clicks for money: Predicting video views through a sentiment analysis of titles and thumbnails
finding: OpenAlex holds no abstract; title and keywords (clickbait, video thumbnails, video titles, click-through rate, sentiment analysis, YouTube, captions, emoticons) show a model predicting video views from the sentiment of titles and thumbnails. No result can be stated from the record.
why_for_us: Candidate source for how emotional tone of the thumbnail and title relates to views; read the full text before writing thumbnail rules.

title: An exploration of the relation between the visual attributes of thumbnails and the view-through of videos: The case of branded video content
finding: OpenAlex holds no abstract; title and keywords (video thumbnails, elaboration likelihood model, central route persuasion, celebrity endorsement, image quality, YouTube, image mining) show an image-mining study relating thumbnail attributes to view-through of branded videos. No result can be stated from the record.
why_for_us: The closest study to our case (thumbnails of branded video and how much of the video is then watched); full text needed for the direction of the effects.

title: Measuring Audience Retention in YouTube
venue: International ICST Conference on Performance Evaluation Methodologies and Tools (VALUETOOLS)
finding: Methodological paper on the audience-retention measures YouTube gives creators: examines consistency between existing measures, asks when a video is too long and would gain from shortening, and proposes a new retention measure. No empirical drop-off figures in the abstract.
why_for_us: Use it to choose which retention metric to track per episode and to decide from the curve whether 90 s should be cut to 60 s; it does not tell us what a good opening looks like.

title: Does Clickbait Actually Attract More Clicks? Three Clickbait Studies You Must Read
venue: CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
finding: Three studies (quasi-experiment with classifier-labelled headlines, controlled experiment varying one clickbait feature on an identical story, analysis of four classifiers on real sharing data): clickbait did not generate more curiosity than non-clickbait in Studies 1-2; the detectors agreed on a classification only 47% of the time, per authors.
why_for_us: Clickbait formulas (lists, questions, teasing phrasing) in titles are not a reliable way to raise interest; no need to risk credibility with notaries for an effect that controlled tests do not find.

title: Seeing is not always believing: an exploratory study of clickbait in WeChat
finding: Longitudinal data from a company running more than 500 WeChat official accounts, text mining plus econometrics: hyperbole, insinuation and visual rhetoric in headlines raise clicks, but the number of clickbait headlines a publisher posts has an inverted U-shaped relation with its visit traffic, moderated by publisher age, per authors.
why_for_us: Baiting can lift single clicks yet too much of it reduces a channel's traffic over time: for a series that needs returning viewers, titles and thumbnails must be kept honest to the episode.

title: Short video marketing: what, when and how short-branded videos facilitate consumer engagement
finding: 10,240 Weibo short videos from 122 brands (238.6 h), coded content plus engagement data: content matching, information relevance, storytelling and emotionality significantly affect likes, comments and shares; release time moderates emotionality - morning release strengthens the positive effect of warmth, excitement and joy versus afternoon, per authors.
why_for_us: Supports the micro-drama form itself (storytelling and emotionality drive engagement in branded short video) and suggests testing morning publication for warm/funny episodes. Engagement, not retention; consumer brands in China.

title: The Science of the First Three Seconds: An Empirical Analysis of Emotional Tone, Rhetorical Style, and Category Norms in Viral TikTok Hooks
finding: Preprint, single author: 46,605 TikTok opening lines from 20+ categories; emotional hooks are rare (about 3.2% of posts) yet draw proportionally more comments and shares; curiosity gaps and urgency statements outperform direct address or 'how to' phrasing in most categories; best hook length varies by niche from about 9 words (news) to about 90 (entertainment), per author.
why_for_us: Only large data set on the wording of the first line: favours a curiosity-gap opening line over 'Dear notaries...' direct address or a how-to promise. Not peer reviewed, engagement rather than watch time - use as a hypothesis.

title: Fleeting Attention While Scrolling: Dwell Time and Exposure in Social Media Feeds
finding: Preprint with preregistered analyses: 43,921 post-viewing episodes from 1,102 participants on a simulated Instagram-like platform; median dwell time 0.93 s; little evidence that visual complexity, valence, arousal, theme, presence of a face or social reinforcement relate to dwell time; dwell falls across the browsing sequence and is considerably longer on profile and explore pages than in the main feed, per authors.
why_for_us: In feed the first frame has under a second, and content features (including a face) barely moved dwell here: make the first frame legible in under 1 s and rely more on placements with longer dwell (profile page, email, direct link). Still images, simulated platform, preprint.

title: Predicting Ad Liking and Purchase Intent: Large-Scale Analysis of Facial Responses to Ads
finding: Webcam facial coding over the internet: over 12,000 responses from 1,223 people to 170 ads; ad liking predicted with ROC AUC = 0.85 and change in purchase intent with AUC = 0.78; per authors peak positive responses immediately preceded by a brand appearance are more likely to be effective.
why_for_us: Timing rule for the brand: show it just before the emotional peak (the punchline or relief), not after and not in a flat moment; applies to the full episode and to where the 15 s cut starts.

title: How to accurately measure attention to video advertising
finding: Lab experiment manipulating high vs low attention to video ads, eight physiological measures compared with EEG and self-report: per authors eye-tracking measures have problems discriminating high from low attention; heart rate discriminated best and also captures attention to sound. Google-funded.
why_for_us: 'Eyes on screen' or viewability is a weak proxy for real attention; when judging openings prefer behavioural outcomes (retention at 3 s, recall) over gaze-based attention scores sold by vendors.

title: How Moment-to-Moment EEG Measures Enhance Ad Effectiveness Evaluation: Peak Emotions during Branding Moments As Key Indicators
finding: EEG plus survey study of advertising indicators: EEG and survey indicators measure different kinds of emotion and attention; momentary EEG indicators outperform aggregated ones, and peak emotion during branding moments is singled out as a key indicator, per authors. No coefficients in the abstract.
why_for_us: Second independent source (with McDuff et al.) that what matters is the emotion at the moment the brand is on screen: script the brand pulse into the high point of the scene.

title: Best Measures of Attention To Creative Tactics in TV Advertising: When Do Attention-Getting Devices Capture or Reduce Attention?
finding: Eye tracking, skin conductance and heart rate recorded for 10 creative devices across more than 100 TV ads with known in-market sales effectiveness; the study documents how each attention measure relates to attention level and type of device. The abstract reports no device-level results.
why_for_us: Key reference for which attention-getting devices actually capture versus reduce attention (the title says some reduce it); results are in the full text only.

title: How Viewer Tuning, Presence, and Attention Respond to Ad Content and Predict Brand Search Lift
finding: Uses passive, continuous in-home measurement of TV viewer presence and attention, distinguishing true ad exposures from ads airing to empty rooms; per title, relates tuning, presence and attention to ad content and to brand search lift. The OpenAlex abstract is one sentence and gives no results.
why_for_us: Top-venue evidence that attention (not mere delivery) is what links to brand search; check full text for which content features moved attention before citing specifics.

title: Measuring Gaining and Holding Attention to Social Media Ads with Viewport Logging: A Validation Study Using Mobile Eye-Tracking
finding: Validation of viewport logging against mobile eye tracking on smartphones in a social media context: the 1-s viewability threshold (gaining attention) and viewport time (holding attention) show high concurrent validity with eye-tracking metrics and predict brand recall, per authors.
why_for_us: Platform metrics we already get (1-s/3-s views, time in view) are defensible stand-ins for gaining and holding attention in feed, so opening variants can be compared without lab tests.

title: How Advertisers Can Keep Mobile Users Engaged and Reduce Video-Ad Blocking: Best Practices for Video-Ad Placement and Delivery Based on Consumer Neuroscience Measures
finding: Lab study with fixations, heart rate, EEG, skin conductance and facial affect during mobile use: per authors three practices led to positive experience with video ads - keeping the user's choice to engage, limiting how disruptive the ad is, and incentivising viewing. Industry co-authored; no sample size in the abstract.
why_for_us: Prefer placements where the viewer chooses to watch (feed, opt-in email link) over forced interruptions for a sceptical audience.

title: Skippable or non-skippable? Pre-roll or mid-roll? Visual attention and effectiveness of in-stream ads
finding: 2x2 between-subjects eye-tracking experiment (skippable/non-skippable x pre-roll/mid-roll): non-skippable and pre-roll ads were superior on visual attention, brand recall and related effectiveness measures; excessive visual attention goes to the skip-button location, per authors. Sample size not in the abstract.
why_for_us: In skippable placements eyes sit on the skip button's corner during the first 5 s: keep the essential early image and caption away from being the only carrier in the opposite corner - centre them. Conflicts with Krishnan & Sitaraman on mid-roll completion.

title: Understanding in-video dropouts and interaction peaks inonline lecture videos
finding: Second-by-second interaction data from 862 videos in four edX MOOCs: higher dropout in longer videos, in re-watching sessions and in tutorials versus lectures; in a sample of 80 videos 61% of interaction peaks accompany visual transitions, per authors.
why_for_us: For viewers who watch to learn something, length itself drives dropout and visual transitions mark the points people return to: keep explainer cuts short and put a clear visual change where the key point sits.

title: Video-based Learning in Surgery: Establishing Surgeon Engagement and Utilization of Variable-duration Videos
finding: Platform data 2011-2017 for 117 nerve-surgery videos (over 3 million views) on YouTube and a surgeon-only site, plus a survey of 304 surgeons: the specialist site reached 48.4% mean engagement (14.3 points above YouTube); engagement declined with video duration; surgeons preferred longer videos for infrequent or difficult cases than for routine ones, per authors.
why_for_us: Rare evidence on an expert professional audience: experts watch more on a dedicated professional channel than on open YouTube and accept length when the case is hard - host episodes on our own page too, and offer short and long versions.

title: Effectiveness of B2B social media marketing: The effect of message source and message content on social media engagement
finding: Four experiments in B2B settings: employee-generated content leads to higher social media engagement than firm-generated content, through content-based and engagement-based trust; emojis help more in employee-generated messages; no evidence that adding objective information raises engagement, per authors.
why_for_us: Publish episodes from a person's profile (founder, a practising notary) rather than only the company page, and do not expect that loading the post or opening with facts and figures will raise engagement.

title: A longitudinal study of B2B customer engagement in LinkedIn: The role of brand personality
finding: 114 weeks of LinkedIn activity of one small consultancy, VARX model: more impressions lead to more likes, clicks and shares, clicks to new followers, followers to impressions; posts higher in excitement increase impressions and likes, in competence increase clicks, in ruggedness increase new followers, per authors. Single-firm case.
why_for_us: On LinkedIn an exciting tone buys reach and a competent tone buys clicks: open the LinkedIn cut with the lively moment and put the competence signal (what exactly the tool does) next to the link. One firm only.

title: Advertising to businesses: Does creativity matter?
finding: OpenAlex holds no abstract; title and keywords (advertising creativity, business-to-business advertising, brand attitude, behavioral intention, advertising effectiveness) show a test of whether creative advertising affects attitudes and intentions of business buyers. No result can be stated from the record.
why_for_us: The direct test of whether a creative (non-rational) approach works on business decision makers; read the full text before arguing for or against a playful opening for notaries.

title: What messages to post? Evaluating the popularity of social media communications in business versus consumer markets
finding: OpenAlex holds no abstract; title and keywords (social media marketing, message appeal, corporate branding, Fortune 500 companies) show a comparison of which message appeals and branding cues make B2B versus B2C social media posts popular. No result can be stated from the record.
why_for_us: Most-cited source on how B2B and B2C audiences differ in response to emotional/functional appeals and brand cues in posts; full text needed for the direction of effects.
